findings.message: The internal key-serving app is bound to `0.0.0.0:8081` instead of `127.0.0.1`. This endpoint has no authentication and returns every user's authorized SSH public keys. While Docker Compose doesn't publish the port, any container in the same Docker network can reach it directly. Binding to `127.0.0.1` would restrict access to processes inside the same container, which is the intended threat model described in the README.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The internal API is factually confirmed to bind on 0.0.0.0:8081 with no authentication. Any container in the same Docker network can enumerate usernames and retrieve permitopen host assignments (internal hostnames/ports). The suggested fix (127.0.0.1) would break the intended two-container deployment shown in ARCHITECTURE.md, but the core concern — unauthenticated endpoint exposing internal network topology to any co-network container — is valid and actionable.
findings.severity_justification: The endpoint leaks internal host topology (permitopen entries with private hostnames and ports) and enables username enumeration to any container in the Docker network. Exposure is limited by Docker network isolation, but the lack of any authentication on a sensitive internal endpoint is a real concern.
findings.category_justification: Unauthenticated endpoint binding on 0.0.0.0 that exposes sensitive internal data (user existence, SSH keys, and internal host topology) to any container in the Docker network.

findings.message: `deactivate_user` has no guard against an admin deactivating their own account, unlike `delete_user` which explicitly blocks self-deletion. A sole admin can POST to `/users/{their_own_id}/deactivate`, setting `is_active=False` on themselves. Because the session middleware checks `user.is_active`, their next request will not resolve a user, and since there are no other admins, the system becomes permanently unmanageable (no admin recovery path exists without direct DB access).
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: deactivate_user has no self-deactivation guard, while delete_user explicitly blocks self-deletion with 'if user.id == user_id'. The session middleware confirms that inactive users are not loaded (checks user.is_active). A sole admin can POST /users/{own_id}/deactivate, immediately losing all admin access with no in-app recovery path.
findings.severity_justification: A sole admin can lock themselves out of the system, requiring direct DB access to recover. While this requires the admin to act on their own account (somewhat self-inflicted), it could also be triggered accidentally from the UI. The system becomes permanently unmanageable without DB access, which is a real operational risk.
findings.category_justification: Logic inconsistency — delete_user has a self-guard but deactivate_user does not, leading to an exploitable state where the system becomes unmanageable.

findings.message: The `POST /totp/verify` endpoint has no rate-limiting decorator. During TOTP enrollment, a user has a valid session (credentials accepted) but no TOTP device. An attacker who has stolen credentials can loop over all 1,000,000 six-digit codes against this endpoint at network speed. The ±1 time-step window means 3 codes are valid per 30-second interval. The absence of a `@limiter.limit(...)` here contrasts with the `5/15minutes` limit on `/login` and leaves this code path completely unbounded.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Confirmed: /login has @limiter.limit('5/15minutes') but POST /totp/verify has no rate-limiting decorator. The endpoint accepts any authenticated-but-not-enrolled session, allowing an attacker with stolen credentials to brute-force TOTP codes at network speed with no throttling.
findings.severity_justification: TOTP is the sole 2FA mechanism protecting all accounts. Without rate limiting on the verification endpoint, an attacker who steals credentials can brute-force the enrollment TOTP at network speed, completely bypassing 2FA. This undermines the core security control of the system.
findings.category_justification: Missing rate limiting on an authentication endpoint allows brute-force attacks that defeat the 2FA mechanism.

findings.message: PBKDF2 key derivation for TOTP secret encryption uses a static, hardcoded salt `b"callis-totp-encryption"`. This salt is the same across every deployment and is public knowledge (it's in source). If an attacker obtains the database and makes a guess at the SECRET_KEY, they can derive the exact Fernet key used across all installations without any per-deployment or per-secret randomness, reducing offline attack cost. The salt should at minimum be randomized per installation (e.g., derived from SECRET_KEY itself or stored separately).
findings.tp_fp_justification: The static salt is a technical best-practice deviation, but the claim that it 'reduces offline attack cost' doesn't hold when the PBKDF2 input (SECRET_KEY) is a properly-generated 256-bit random value as documented. Precomputation against a 2^256 keyspace is infeasible regardless of salt. The concern is only meaningful for weak/low-entropy SECRET_KEYs, which the documentation explicitly guards against. The suggested fix ('derived from SECRET_KEY itself') would add zero security.
findings.severity_justification: Theoretical best-practice deviation with negligible practical impact when SECRET_KEY is properly generated as documented.
findings.category_justification: The finding concerns cryptographic key derivation practices.

findings.message: The SSH key `label` form field has no server-side length validation before the INSERT. `SSHKey.label` is a `String(255)` column: SQLite silently stores any length, but PostgreSQL will raise a database-level `DataError` for labels longer than 255 characters, which propagates as an unhandled 500 error. The same pattern applies to `display_name` and `email` in `create_user`, and `label`/`description` in `create_host`. A `len()` guard before the DB write would keep behavior consistent across backends.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Confirmed: SSHKey.label is String(255) with no server-side length guard before INSERT. The only len() checks in users.py are for password minimum length. hosts.py validates hostname length but not label/description. PostgreSQL would raise DataError (→ unhandled 500) on inputs >255 chars while SQLite silently stores them, creating backend-inconsistent behavior.
findings.severity_justification: Only affects PostgreSQL deployments and only when users submit unusually long labels. Primary backend is SQLite (default). The impact is an unhandled 500 instead of a 400, which is poor UX but not a security or data integrity issue. The fix is straightforward but non-urgent.
findings.category_justification: Backend-inconsistent behavior: the same input causes silent success on SQLite but an unhandled 500 on PostgreSQL due to missing length validation.

findings.message: `create_host` validates `hostname` and `port` but does not validate `label` length. `Host.label` is `String(255)`, so a label longer than 255 characters will silently succeed on SQLite but raise an unhandled database error on PostgreSQL. Additionally, the unvalidated `label` is included verbatim in the audit log `detail` dict; a very long label there bloats the JSON column.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Confirmed: create_host validates hostname (regex + len > 255) and port range, but label has no length validation before INSERT. Host.label is String(255). The raw label is also written verbatim into the audit log JSON. The SQLite/PostgreSQL behavior inconsistency claim is accurate.
findings.severity_justification: Same as finding 5: only affects PostgreSQL deployments and only on abnormally long labels. Primary backend is SQLite. The audit log bloat claim is real but marginal. Not a security issue.
findings.category_justification: Missing input validation causing backend-inconsistent behavior (silent success on SQLite, unhandled DB error on PostgreSQL).

findings.message: TOTP secret generation in `totp_setup_page` has a TOCTOU race: two concurrent GET requests for the same unenrolled user will both observe `db_user.totp_secret is None`, each generate a different random secret, and both attempt to flush. The last writer wins; the user scanning the QR code from the first response will have set up their authenticator against a secret that is then overwritten, causing all subsequent TOTP verifications to fail permanently. A `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` or unique constraint would close this window.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The race condition is real and correctly described. Both concurrent requests load totp_secret=None, generate different secrets, and flush; last writer wins while the user holds the QR from the first response. The code reuses an existing secret only if it's already set, providing no protection against concurrent initial requests.
findings.severity_justification: Race window is extremely narrow (first-visit only, concurrent requests from same user required), making this practically unlikely. The consequence is user lockout (not a security bypass), and it requires direct DB access to recover — bad UX but low probability.
findings.category_justification: TOCTOU race in TOTP secret initialization — concurrent requests can overwrite each other's generated secrets, causing permanent TOTP failure for the affected user.

findings.message: The internal `/internal/keys/{username}` endpoint performs no input validation on the `username` path parameter. While the SQL query is parameterized (no injection risk), a caller that bypasses `auth-keys.sh` can send arbitrarily long or malformed strings. Since `auth-keys.sh` enforces the regex `^[a-z][a-z0-9_-]{0,31}$` before calling the API, the endpoint itself should apply the same check and return 400/empty for non-conforming values, enforcing defense-in-depth given the endpoint is accessible to any container in the Docker network.
findings.tp_fp_justification: While factually correct that no username validation exists on the endpoint, there is no concrete exploitable outcome: malformed usernames simply fail the DB lookup and return an empty 200 — identical behavior to a validated rejection. The SQL is parameterized, there's no crash path, and no sensitive data is leaked. This is a defense-in-depth style recommendation without a demonstrated concrete vulnerability.
findings.severity_justification: No injection risk, no crash, no sensitive data leak from malformed inputs. The missing validation has no practical security consequence given how the endpoint already handles non-matching inputs.
findings.category_justification: The finding frames this as a defense-in-depth security concern on an unauthenticated internal endpoint.

findings.message: The session middleware loads the `User` object inside a short-lived `async with factory() as db` block and stores it in `request.state.user`. The SQLAlchemy session is then closed, leaving the user object detached. The ORM relationships `ssh_keys` and `assigned_hosts` are lazy-loaded by default; any code that accesses `request.state.user.ssh_keys` or `.assigned_hosts` outside a session context will either silently return an empty collection or raise a `MissingGreenlet`/`DetachedInstanceError`. Routes that need those relationships correctly reload the user with `selectinload`, but this is an easy footgun for future contributors.
findings.tp_fp_justification: All technical claims verified: the User is loaded in a closed session (detached), relationships are default lazy-loaded, and accessing them outside a session in SQLAlchemy async would raise MissingGreenlet. Current code avoids the bug by using selectinload in routes that need relationships, and templates only access scalar attributes. The finding correctly identifies this as a latent footgun even though nothing is currently broken.
findings.severity_justification: No current broken behavior — all active code paths correctly handle the detached user. The risk is future contributor error, not an existing bug. The pattern is fragile but the codebase consistently works around it today.
findings.category_justification: Architectural footgun for future contributors: detached ORM object with lazy relationships stored in request state, with no enforcement (e.g., lazy='raise') to catch accidental relationship access.

findings.message: `delete_user` prevents self-deletion but does not check whether deleting the target would leave zero active admin accounts. An admin (A) can delete another admin (B) leaving A as the last admin; A cannot delete themselves, so the last admin can never be removed — but deactivation (finding #2) achieves the same outcome without this guard. The two endpoints should share consistent protection: block operations that would leave no active admin in the system.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The factual claim about missing 'last admin' protection in delete_user is correct and the inconsistency with deactivate_user is real. However, delete_user cannot itself produce a zero-admin state since self-deletion is blocked. The finding correctly notes the real vector is deactivation (finding 2), making this a consistency concern rather than a standalone bug.
findings.severity_justification: delete_user alone cannot produce a zero-admin state; the lockout path requires combining deletion of other admins with the deactivate_user gap from finding 2. The finding identifies a conceptual inconsistency rather than an additional attack surface beyond finding 2.
findings.category_justification: Inconsistent guard logic between two endpoints performing similar privileged operations (delete vs deactivate user).

findings.message: The `user_detail` route does not have a `require_totp_complete` dependency. This allows a user who has not completed 2FA setup to access their profile page by navigating directly to `/users/{user_id}` after logging in. While they cannot perform actions, they can view the page, which is inconsistent with the application's security policy of gating all pages behind TOTP enrollment.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The finding is incorrect. require_admin_or_self explicitly depends on require_totp_complete (verified in dependencies.py), so TOTP is enforced in the dependency chain. Additionally, TOTPGuardMiddleware intercepts all non-exempt paths at the middleware level, redirecting unenrolled users before the route handler executes. The route has double TOTP protection.
findings.severity_justification: No actual security gap exists — the claim is factually wrong.
findings.category_justification: Finding concerns TOTP enforcement policy on a route.

findings.message: The `host_list` route uses `@router.get("/hosts")` without explicitly depending on `require_totp_complete`. While access is indirectly protected for logged-in users by the `require_totp_complete` dependency on `user`, this protection is not applied to users who have not yet enrolled in TOTP. A user can log in, not set up TOTP, and still access the `/hosts` page by navigating to it directly, which violates the application's stated security requirement that all pages are locked until TOTP is configured.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The finding is incorrect. host_list explicitly depends on require_totp_complete at line 26: 'user: User = Depends(require_totp_complete)'. Additionally, TOTPGuardMiddleware enforces TOTP at the middleware level for all non-exempt paths. Both layers are present.
findings.severity_justification: No actual security gap — the claim is factually wrong.
findings.category_justification: Finding concerns TOTP enforcement policy on a route.

findings.message: In the `/login` endpoint, an audit log for `LOGIN_FAILURE` is written with `actor_id=None` even when the user is found. This makes it harder to track failed login attempts for specific users. The `user.id` is available but not passed to `write_audit_log`.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The claim that user.id 'is not passed' is factually incorrect. For the wrong_password failure path, target_id=user.id is explicitly set. Using actor_id=None for failed authentication is also semantically correct — the actor_id field represents an authenticated actor, not a claimed identity. The user-not-found case correctly uses None since no user can be identified.
findings.severity_justification: No actual audit logging gap exists; user identity is captured correctly via target_id for found-user failure cases.
findings.category_justification: Finding makes an incorrect factual claim about what data is passed to write_audit_log.

findings.message: In the `/login` endpoint, an audit log for `TOTP_FAILURE` is written with `actor_id=None` even though the user has been successfully authenticated with their password and the user object is available. This makes it difficult to correlate failed 2FA attempts with the specific user who was trying to log in.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The TOTP_FAILURE audit log explicitly sets target_id=user.id and detail includes target_username. The user is fully identifiable in the log. The claim that correlation is difficult is factually incorrect. Using actor_id=None for incomplete authentication (TOTP not yet verified) is semantically correct.
findings.severity_justification: No actual audit logging gap — the user identity is captured via target_id and detail fields.
findings.category_justification: Finding makes an incorrect factual claim about audit log content.

findings.message: The `/audit` route does not correctly apply the `require_totp_complete` dependency for non-admin users with the `readonly` role. The `require_role("readonly")` check includes `require_totp_complete`, but it is applied *after* a user object is passed in. A `readonly` user who has not completed TOTP setup can bypass the 2FA requirement and view the audit log page by navigating to `/audit` directly after login.
findings.tp_fp_justification: require_role('readonly') explicitly depends on require_totp_complete in its inner _check function (verified in dependencies.py). Additionally, TOTPGuardMiddleware redirects any unenrolled user away from /audit at the middleware level before the route is reached. The route has dual TOTP protection.
findings.severity_justification: No actual security gap — the claim is factually incorrect on both the dependency chain and middleware levels.
findings.category_justification: Finding concerns TOTP enforcement policy on a route.

findings.message: The `onSuccess` function inside the copy-to-clipboard handler directly mutates the `textContent` of the button. This can cause a layout shift if the new text ("Copied!") is wider or narrower than the original text, and it's not ideal for accessibility. A better approach would be to use CSS classes to show/hide a separate status indicator or use ARIA attributes to announce the success.
findings.tp_fp_justification: While the finding is factually correct that textContent is mutated directly, this is a standard and widely-used pattern for clipboard copy feedback across the web. The 'layout shift' concern is negligible for a small utility button, and the same pattern (temp text swap) is used in countless production UIs including GitHub. The finding restates a general UX/a11y best practice without identifying a concrete, specific problem in this codebase — it could be copy-pasted onto any project using this common pattern.
findings.severity_justification: Cosmetic/UX concern with negligible real-world impact. No functional bug, no security issue, no data loss.
findings.category_justification: The finding's primary concerns are layout shift and accessibility (ARIA announcements) for the clipboard feedback mechanism.

findings.message: The `change` event listener for host user assignment constructs a URL for an htmx POST request but does not sanitize or validate `sel.value`. Since `sel.value` is taken directly from the `value` attribute of a `<select>` option, a maliciously crafted response or DOM manipulation could inject characters that break out of the URL path, potentially leading to misdirected requests. While the user IDs are UUIDs, making exploitation difficult, it's safer to validate that the value matches the expected format of a UUID.
findings.tp_fp_justification: sel.value comes from server-rendered UUID option values. The attack requires either server compromise or DOM XSS, both blocked by existing CSP and both implying pre-existing full control. Server-side UUID lookup handles unexpected values with 404. The finding acknowledges UUIDs make exploitation difficult and presents no concrete exploitable path.
findings.severity_justification: No realistic attack path given UUIDs as values, CSP preventing XSS, and server-side validation.
findings.category_justification: Finding concerns client-side URL construction and potential path injection.

findings.message: The TOTP verification logic incorrectly normalizes invalid codes to `"000000"` before comparison. This means that if a user submits a non-digit or wrong-length code, the system will perform a constant-time comparison against a dummy code instead of the real expected TOTP code. While the `valid_format` check at the end prevents a successful login, this behavior is unnecessary and could introduce subtle timing differences if the comparison path for a dummy code differs from a real one. The comparison should be skipped entirely if the format is invalid.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The normalization to '000000' is intentional constant-time design (noted in the code comment). secrets.compare_digest runs in constant time regardless of inputs, and comparing equal-length strings ('000000' vs any 6-digit code) eliminates timing differences. The suggested fix (skip comparison for invalid format) would create a fast-path timing oracle distinguishing invalid-format from valid-format-wrong codes, which is worse than the current approach.
findings.severity_justification: No actual vulnerability — the current design is more secure than the suggested alternative.
findings.category_justification: Finding concerns timing side-channels in TOTP verification.

findings.message: The `register_template_filters` function is called directly on the `templates` instance in `main.py`, `routers/users.py`, `routers/hosts.py`, `routers/audit.py`, and `routers/auth.py`. This repeated registration is redundant. The filters should be registered only once on the main `templates` instance in `main.py` before it is used by any routers.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Each router module creates its own Jinja2Templates instance (verified: 5 separate instances across main.py and 4 routers). register_template_filters must be called on each independent instance. Registering only on main.py's instance would leave router templates without the slugify filter and app_version global, breaking SSH config template rendering.
findings.severity_justification: The finding is incorrect; implementing its suggestion would introduce a bug.
findings.category_justification: Finding concerns code organization and DRY principles around template filter registration.

findings.message: The query to fetch the key counts executes one SQL query for all users initially, but the loop updates the key_counts dictionary by iterating through query results in Python. This can be an inefficiency if users with many keys dominate the dataset, as aggregation computation cost is shifted to SQL execution and iteration. Reexamine key_count computation logic for scalability.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The code uses a single GROUP BY aggregate query (correctly noted in the code comment as avoiding N+1). SQL aggregation is the correct approach here. The Python iteration is O(rows returned) which equals the number of distinct users with active keys — trivially fast. The finding's concern about SQL aggregation cost is backwards; SQL GROUP BY is more efficient than any Python-side alternative.
findings.severity_justification: No actual inefficiency exists — the implementation is correct and well-optimized.
findings.category_justification: Finding concerns query efficiency and scalability of key count computation.

findings.message: [dockerfile.security.missing-user-entrypoint.missing-user-entrypoint] By not specifying a USER, a program in the container may run as 'root'. This is a security hazard. If an attacker can control a process running as root, they may have control over the container. Ensure that the last USER in a Dockerfile is a USER other than 'root'.
findings.tp_fp_justification: This is a verbatim boilerplate scanner output that ignores application requirements. The Dockerfile runs OpenSSH sshd which architecturally requires root (port 22 binding, privilege separation, AuthorizedKeysCommandUser root for dynamic OS user creation). The finding provides no concrete exploitable path and could be copy-pasted onto any rootless Dockerfile finding.
findings.severity_justification: Running as root is architecturally required for sshd and dynamic user management; the generic recommendation doesn't apply here.
findings.category_justification: Finding concerns container privilege escalation risk from running as root.

findings.message: [dockerfile.security.missing-user.missing-user] By not specifying a USER, a program in the container may run as 'root'. This is a security hazard. If an attacker can control a process running as root, they may have control over the container. Ensure that the last USER in a Dockerfile is a USER other than 'root'.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Same boilerplate scanner output as finding 21. While api/Dockerfile has no architectural need for root (unlike the sshd Dockerfile), the finding provides no concrete exploit path — it's identical template text that fires on any Dockerfile without a USER directive. The hardening recommendation is valid but the finding is generic.
findings.severity_justification: Running the API as root in a container is suboptimal hardening, but requires application compromise first to matter. The actual risk is low in a containerized environment.
findings.category_justification: Finding concerns container privilege escalation risk from running as root.

findings.message: [html.security.audit.missing-integrity.missing-integrity] This tag is missing an 'integrity' subresource integrity attribute. The 'integrity' attribute allows for the browser to verify that externally hosted files (for example from a CDN) are delivered without unexpected manipulation. Without this attribute, if an attacker can modify the externally hosted resource, this could lead to XSS and other types of attacks. To prevent this, include the base64-encoded cryptographic hash of the resource (file) you’re telling the browser to fetch in the 'integrity' attribute for all externally hosted files.
findings.tp_fp_justification: This is a verbatim boilerplate scanner output (rule ID format: [html.security.audit.missing-integrity.missing-integrity]) that fires on any external resource tag without an integrity attribute. It names no specific hash, no specific CDN compromise scenario, and is identical generic text that would apply to any HTML file loading from a CDN. No concrete exploitable vulnerability is demonstrated.
findings.severity_justification: SRI is a valid hardening measure but the finding demonstrates no concrete attack path against this specific application.
findings.category_justification: Finding concerns subresource integrity and potential CDN-based XSS.

findings.message: [python.django.security.django-no-csrf-token.django-no-csrf-token] Manually-created forms in django templates should specify a csrf_token to prevent CSRF attacks.
findings.tp_fp_justification: This is a Django CSRF rule incorrectly applied to a FastAPI/Jinja2 application. The project uses FastAPI, not Django — there is no Django CSRF middleware, no {% csrf_token %} template tag available, and the rule does not apply. CSRF protection in this app is handled by SameSite=strict session cookies, which is a valid CSRF mitigation for same-site form submissions.
findings.severity_justification: Wrong framework rule applied — completely inapplicable to this codebase.
findings.category_justification: Finding concerns CSRF protection on HTML forms.

findings.message: [dockerfile.security.missing-user-entrypoint.missing-user-entrypoint] By not specifying a USER, a program in the container may run as 'root'. This is a security hazard. If an attacker can control a process running as root, they may have control over the container. Ensure that the last USER in a Dockerfile is a USER other than 'root'.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Same verbatim boilerplate scanner output as findings 21 and 22. The sshd/Dockerfile runs OpenSSH sshd which architecturally requires root: it binds port 22, performs SSH privilege separation, and auth-keys.sh uses AuthorizedKeysCommandUser root for dynamic OS user creation. Running as non-root would break core functionality. No concrete exploit path demonstrated.
findings.severity_justification: Running as root is architecturally required for sshd operation; the generic recommendation does not apply.
findings.category_justification: Finding concerns container privilege escalation risk from running as root.

findings.message: This documents `AUTH_MODE=oidc` as supported, but the application only defines the setting and has no OIDC implementation or routes; `AUTH_MODE` is not used anywhere in `api/`. Users who set this value will still get local-password login behavior.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: AUTH_MODE is defined in core.py Settings but is never read or checked anywhere in the api/ codebase. The README at line 257 documents 'local or oidc' as valid values, misleading users into thinking OIDC is a functional option when it silently does nothing.
findings.severity_justification: No security or correctness harm — users who set AUTH_MODE=oidc just get local auth unchanged. The issue is misleading documentation, not broken behavior.
findings.category_justification: The core problem is that the README documents a feature (AUTH_MODE=oidc) that has no implementation, making it a documentation accuracy issue.

findings.message: This example tells users to use the `postgresql+asyncpg` driver, but `asyncpg` is not included in `api/pyproject.toml`, so deployments using this documented URL will fail at startup with a missing driver unless they rebuild with an extra dependency.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: asyncpg is not in api/pyproject.toml dependencies, but .env.example line 27 documents 'postgresql+asyncpg://user:pass@host:5432/callis' as the PostgreSQL URL. A deployment following this documentation would fail at startup with a missing driver error.
findings.severity_justification: Any user attempting PostgreSQL deployment following the documented example will get a startup failure. SQLite (the default) works fine, but the PostgreSQL path is broken as documented.
findings.category_justification: Missing dependency causes a runtime startup failure for a documented deployment configuration.

findings.message: This exposes the internal key endpoint port in the API image even though the endpoint is unauthenticated and documented as Docker-network-only. With `docker run -P` or platforms that publish exposed ports automatically, `/internal/keys/{username}` can become reachable externally; avoid exposing 8081 from the public image.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: api/Dockerfile line 23 has 'EXPOSE 8080 8081'. The internal endpoint on 8081 is completely unauthenticated and returns SSH keys plus internal host/port assignments (via permitopen options) for any username. docker-compose.yml correctly doesn't publish 8081, but EXPOSE signals publishability and tools using docker run -P or auto-publish platforms would expose it.
findings.severity_justification: The endpoint is unauthenticated and leaks internal hostnames, ports, and user existence. While SSH public keys are not secrets themselves, the internal network topology exposed via permitopen options is sensitive. Exploitation requires non-default deployment patterns (docker run -P or auto-publishing platforms).
findings.category_justification: Exposing an unauthenticated endpoint that leaks internal infrastructure topology is a security concern.

findings.message: This route returns every configured host to any authenticated user with completed TOTP. Since host assignments are the access boundary and hostnames/IPs are internal infrastructure details, non-admin users should only receive hosts assigned to them (or the route should be admin-only) rather than all hosts.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: the GET /hosts route (lines 23-46) uses require_totp_complete (any authenticated user) and fetches all Host records with no assignment filter. The template renders every host's label, hostname, and port to all users. A readonly user sees all internal infrastructure details regardless of their assignments.
findings.severity_justification: Internal hostnames and IPs are leaked to all authenticated users, not just those assigned to those hosts. This violates the documented access boundary (users can only jump to assigned hosts), though it doesn't grant actual SSH access to unassigned hosts.
findings.category_justification: Information disclosure — internal network topology (hostnames, ports) visible to users who should not have access to those hosts.

findings.message: Required secrets are only typed as strings, so `.env` entries like `SECRET_KEY=` or `ADMIN_PASSWORD=` satisfy settings validation. That allows the app to start with an empty JWT/TOTP encryption secret and/or create the initial admin with an empty password; enforce non-empty minimum lengths before startup.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: SECRET_KEY and ADMIN_PASSWORD are typed as plain str with no validators, min_length, or field_validator. An empty value (e.g. SECRET_KEY= in .env) passes validation. The app would start with an empty JWT signing/TOTP encryption key and an empty admin password.
findings.severity_justification: An empty SECRET_KEY allows any JWT to be forged (anyone can authenticate as any user). An empty ADMIN_PASSWORD lets anyone log in as admin without a password. Both are critical security failures that can be triggered by a misconfigured .env.
findings.category_justification: Missing input validation on security-critical secrets allows the application to start in an insecure state where authentication can be bypassed.

findings.message: This relies on `AuthorizedKeysCommand` to create the OS account, but sshd performs the account lookup before public-key authorization and will not authenticate a username that does not already exist locally. Since this is the only user-creation path in the repository, newly created Callis users will be rejected as invalid users before this script can create their OS account.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: auth-keys.sh is the only user creation path. In modern OpenSSH, a fake passwd entry is created for unknown users before AuthorizedKeysCommand is called; even if the script creates the OS user and returns keys, sshd already has a stale/fake pw entry and auth fails on the first attempt. New users must connect twice, which breaks the expected first-login experience and is contrary to the script's stated intent.
findings.severity_justification: The core product function is SSH jump access. New users will always fail their first SSH connection attempt, requiring a retry before access works. This is a correctness failure in the primary feature.
findings.category_justification: The design of on-the-fly OS user creation via AuthorizedKeysCommand is fundamentally incompatible with OpenSSH's user validation ordering, causing first-connection failures.

findings.message: The rate limiter keys only on `request.client.host`. In the documented reverse-proxy deployment mode, all clients appear as the proxy address because there is no trusted proxy/X-Forwarded-For handling, so one user's failed logins can rate-limit everyone behind that proxy and audit source IPs will be inaccurate.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: the limiter uses slowapi's get_remote_address which reads request.client.host (TCP peer). No ProxyHeadersMiddleware or X-Forwarded-For handling exists anywhere in the codebase. The README documents a reverse-proxy deployment mode. Both rate limiting and audit source_ip logging would see only the proxy address, not actual client IPs.
findings.severity_justification: In proxy deployments, a single attacker's login attempts exhaust the rate limit for all users behind the proxy — undermining the brute-force protection entirely. Audit IPs are also inaccurate. The LAN-only mode is unaffected.
findings.category_justification: Broken rate limiting in proxy mode undermines brute-force protection, a documented security control.

findings.message: `last_used_at` is displayed here, but the field is never updated anywhere in the SSH authentication/key lookup path (the only references are this template and the partial). This will always show `Never`, which is misleading for users and admins.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: last_used_at exists in the model and is rendered in two templates, but there is no code anywhere in the codebase that updates this field. The internal key lookup path (routers/internal.py) never sets it. It will always display 'Never'.
findings.severity_justification: Misleading UI that shows stale data, but does not affect security or core functionality. Users and admins simply can't track key usage.
findings.category_justification: A field is displayed as a feature but is never populated, making the displayed value permanently incorrect.

findings.message: `last_used_at` is rendered in this refreshed key list, but no code updates that column during SSH key lookup or login; after HTMX updates this value will still always be `Never` even for keys that have been used.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: same root cause as Finding 8 — last_used_at is never updated anywhere in the codebase. This template (partials/key_list.html line 21) renders the field the same way as user_detail.html, and will always show 'Never'. The claim is factually correct.
findings.severity_justification: Same as Finding 8 — misleading UI with no security or functional impact beyond inaccurate display.
findings.category_justification: Field displayed in UI is never populated, making the value permanently incorrect.

findings.message: The bastion snippet sets `IdentityFile` but not `IdentitiesOnly yes`. Because the bundled sshd config limits `MaxAuthTries` to 2, clients with multiple agent keys can be disconnected before the configured key is tried, making the generated config unreliable for common developer setups.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: ssh_config.html generates a bastion block with IdentityFile but no IdentitiesOnly yes. sshd_config confirms MaxAuthTries 2. SSH clients with multiple agent keys will exhaust both tries with wrong keys before the configured IdentityFile is attempted, causing reliable connection failures for common developer setups.
findings.severity_justification: The generated SSH config — the primary user-facing output of the new feature — will silently fail for users with ssh-agent loaded with multiple keys. This directly undermines the feature's usability.
findings.category_justification: The generated configuration is incorrect/incomplete for a common use case, causing connection failures.

findings.message: This bastion-only snippet also needs `IdentitiesOnly yes`; otherwise clients with several agent keys can hit the server's `MaxAuthTries 2` limit before using the specified `IdentityFile`.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: the else-branch snippet (lines 48-52) also generates IdentityFile without IdentitiesOnly yes, subject to the same MaxAuthTries 2 exhaustion issue as Finding 10. The claim is factually correct for this separate code path.
findings.severity_justification: Same impact as Finding 10 — generated config silently fails for users with multiple agent keys. Affects the bastion-only code path as well.
findings.category_justification: Same root cause as Finding 10: incomplete generated SSH config causes connection failures for a common developer setup.

findings.message: This SSH config snippet sets an `IdentityFile` but not `IdentitiesOnly yes`. With the server's `MaxAuthTries 2`, users who have multiple keys loaded in their SSH agent may be rejected before this identity is attempted.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: dashboard.html lines 24-28 render an SSH config snippet with IdentityFile but no IdentitiesOnly yes. Same MaxAuthTries 2 issue applies. The claim is factually correct for this third distinct template location.
findings.severity_justification: Same impact as Findings 10 and 11 — generated config fails silently for users with multiple agent keys. The dashboard is the first page users see, making this a high-visibility instance.
findings.category_justification: Same root cause as Findings 10/11: incomplete SSH config snippet causes connection failures for common developer setups.

findings.message: The generated target host blocks omit a `User` directive, and the Host model/form has no field for the downstream SSH username. As a result `ssh <alias>` will use the client's local OS username, so these snippets are not actually ready-to-use for targets that require usernames like `ubuntu`, `ec2-user`, or `root`.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: the Host model has no username field and the generated target host blocks in ssh_config.html lines 16-19 omit a User directive. The bastion block sets User to the Callis username but the ProxyJump target blocks do not, so ssh <alias> falls back to the client's local OS username. The template claims to produce ready-to-use config.
findings.severity_justification: A real usability gap — the generated config will often not work out of the box for common targets like ubuntu@server or ec2-user@server — but it's a missing convenience feature rather than a security or correctness failure. Users can manually add the User directive.
findings.category_justification: The feature is advertised as generating ready-to-use SSH config but the generated output is incomplete for the common case of non-local-username targets.

findings.message: These per-host snippets also omit the downstream SSH `User`, so copying an individual block will default to the client's local username rather than the account required on the target host.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: the per-host copy snippets (lines 33-36) only contain HostName, Port, and ProxyJump with no User directive. Same root cause as Finding 13 — Host model has no username field. The claim is factually correct for this separate code path.
findings.severity_justification: Same impact as Finding 13 — individual host snippets advertised as copy-paste-ready will default to the local OS username, which is wrong for most targets.
findings.category_justification: Same root cause as Finding 13: generated SSH config is incomplete, omitting the User directive for target hosts.

findings.message: The host-list SSH snippet omits the downstream `User` directive as well, so `ssh <alias>` will default to the local client username and fail for targets that require a different login user.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: hosts.html lines 92-95 render a snippet with HostName, Port, and ProxyJump but no User directive. Same missing Host.username field as Findings 13 and 14. The claim is factually correct.
findings.severity_justification: Same impact as Findings 13 and 14 — snippet defaults to local OS username for the target host.
findings.category_justification: Same root cause as Findings 13/14: generated SSH config snippet omits User directive for target hosts.

findings.message: This refreshed host-row snippet omits the downstream `User` directive, so the copied alias will use the client's local username instead of the target host's required SSH account.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: host_row.html lines 39-42 render a snippet with HostName, Port, and ProxyJump but no User directive. Same missing Host.username field as Findings 13-15. The claim is factually correct.
findings.severity_justification: Same impact as Findings 13-15 — snippet defaults to local OS username for the target host.
findings.category_justification: Same root cause as Findings 13-15: generated SSH config snippet omits User directive for target hosts.
